case.objective: Investigate a small persistent residual acceleration found in long-term Doppler tracking of two deep-space spacecraft.

observations.observation: Two deep-space spacecraft show a small persistent acceleration residual in trajectory fits.
The residual is approximately directed toward the Sun in the commonly reported analysis, although its direction is not perfectly determined.
The effect is small and persists over long tracking intervals.
The two spacecraft have broadly similar designs and both contain radioisotope power systems.
The spacecraft continuously reject substantial internal heat into space.
The spacecraft geometry includes a large high-gain antenna and other surfaces that can emit or reflect thermal radiation asymmetrically.
The apparent residual changes gradually over time rather than behaving as an obviously random measurement offset.
The navigation model includes known gravitational and spacecraft forces, leaving a residual not initially explained by the model.

constraints: Test spacecraft-systematic explanations before proposing new physics.
Do not assume that a correlation proves causation.
Every major hypothesis must specify evidence that could falsify it.
If the supplied evidence is insufficient for a conclusion, state what measurement is needed.

established_observations: Two deep-space spacecraft show a small persistent acceleration residual in trajectory fits (P-01).
The effect is small and persists over long tracking intervals (P-03).
The two spacecraft have broadly similar designs and both contain radioisotope power systems (P-04).
The spacecraft continuously reject substantial internal heat into space (P-05).
The spacecraft geometry includes a large high-gain antenna and other surfaces that can emit or reflect thermal radiation asymmetrically (P-06).
The apparent residual changes gradually over time rather than behaving as an obviously random measurement offset (P-07).
The navigation model includes known gravitational and spacecraft forces, leaving a residual not initially explained by the model (P-08).
important_clues: The acceleration residual changes gradually over time rather than behaving randomly (P-07), pointing to a systematic process rather than random measurement noise.
Both spacecraft share common physical features: radioisotope power systems, heat rejection, and asymmetric structural geometry (P-04, P-05, P-06).
The trajectory anomaly persists across both deep-space spacecraft despite modeling known forces (P-01, P-04, P-08).
relationships: Internal heat rejection (P-05) generated by radioisotope power systems (P-04) interacts with asymmetric structural geometry (P-06).
The unmodeled trajectory residual (P-01, P-08) exhibits long-term persistence (P-03) and gradual temporal change (P-07).
The persistent trajectory residual (P-01) is associated with an directional estimate that is approximately Sun-pointing (P-02).
uncertainties: The precise directional vector of the residual acceleration is not perfectly determined (P-02).
The precise physical origin of the trajectory residual is not explained by the initial navigation model (P-08).
discriminating_evidence: High-precision vector determination to distinguish whether the residual acceleration points strictly toward the Sun, toward Earth, along the spacecraft spin axis, or along the velocity vector.
Quantitative modeling and historical telemetry analysis of internal thermal dissipation and radiation patterns to test if thermal recoil accounts for the residual magnitude and time dependence.
Correlation analysis comparing the temporal change rate of the residual acceleration with the decay curve of the radioisotope power sources.
Comparative tracking of spacecraft with differing structural geometries, orientations, or thermal dissipation configurations.

core_anomalies: A small persistent acceleration residual remains in trajectory fits for two deep-space spacecraft despite modeling known gravitational and spacecraft forces (P-01, P-03, P-08).
The precise directional vector of the residual acceleration is not fully determined, known only to be approximately Sun-pointing (P-02).
unexpected_patterns: The trajectory acceleration residual changes gradually over time across long tracking intervals rather than behaving as random measurement noise (P-03, P-07).
The trajectory anomaly appears consistently across two distinct deep-space spacecraft sharing similar physical design characteristics (P-01, P-04).
possible_relationships_to_investigate: The interaction between continuous internal heat rejection from radioisotope power systems and asymmetric structural geometry (e.g., high-gain antenna) (P-04, P-05, P-06).
The rate of temporal change in the acceleration residual compared to the decay characteristics of the internal radioisotope power sources (P-04, P-07).
The exact directional vector alignment of the residual acceleration relative to the spacecraft spin axis, Sun direction, Earth direction, or velocity vector (P-02, P-06).
contradictions_or_tensions: Tension between the complete force model used in standard navigation and the observed physical trajectory residuals that persist unaccounted for (P-01, P-08).
Ambiguity regarding whether the vector of acceleration points strictly along an environmental vector (Sun/Earth) or a spacecraft-fixed vector (spin axis/velocity) (P-02).
questions_for_hypothesis_agent: Can asymmetric thermal radiation pressure account for both the observed magnitude and the gradual temporal evolution of the trajectory residual?
Is the observed residual caused by an onboard systematic physical process or an unmodeled external environmental force?
Does the directional vector of the acceleration residual align precisely with the spacecraft's physical geometry and spin axis, or with external reference points like the Sun or Earth?
Does the temporal decay rate of the acceleration residual match the thermal and power output decay rates of the radioisotope systems?

hypotheses.name: Onboard Asymmetric Thermal Radiation Recoil
hypotheses.explanation: Heat produced continuously by internal radioisotope power systems radiates asymmetrically after reflecting off spacecraft structural components (such as the high-gain antenna), exerting a net directional thermal recoil force along the spacecraft's spin axis.
supporting_evidence: The residual acceleration appears consistently across two distinct spacecraft that share similar physical design characteristics (P-01, P-04).

The trajectory residual undergoes a gradual temporal change over long tracking intervals (P-03, P-07), which correlates with the expected thermal output decay of internal radioisotope power sources (P-04, P-07).
The residual vector is approximately Sun-pointing (P-02), which aligns generally with the spin-axis direction of spacecraft oriented toward the inner solar system (P-06).
contradicting_evidence: Existing standard force models have not yet demonstrated complete numerical resolution of the residual magnitude (P-01, P-08).
The exact directional vector of the acceleration is currently ambiguous and not fully determined between a spacecraft-fixed frame (spin axis) and an external environmental frame (P-02, P-06).
hypotheses.discriminating_test: Construct a high-fidelity physical thermal model of heat reflection off the structural geometry and test if its predicted directional force vector rotates strictly with the spacecraft spin axis and decays at a rate matching the radioisotope power decay (P-02, P-04, P-06, P-07).

hypotheses.name: Continuous Low-Level Propellant Leakage or Outgassing
hypotheses.explanation: A small, unmodeled continuous leak from the propulsion system or outgassing of volatile materials generates a persistent recoil force acting on the spacecraft trajectory.
supporting_evidence: Unmodeled physical mass expulsion accounts for small, continuous acceleration residuals beyond standard force models (P-01, P-08).
Outgassing or leakage rates can evolve gradually over multi-year tracking intervals (P-03, P-07).
contradicting_evidence: The anomaly appears consistently across two separate spacecraft (P-01, P-04), which would require nearly identical leak rates and directional orientations across both independent vehicles.
Available data is currently insufficient to confirm active propellant valve leakage or corresponding pressure drops on either spacecraft.
hypotheses.discriminating_test: Correlate telemetry records of propulsion system pressures, attitude control thruster firings, and structural outgassing profiles against trajectory residual changes across both spacecraft (P-01, P-04, P-07).

hypotheses.name: Unmodeled External Interplanetary Environmental Force
hypotheses.explanation: An unmodeled external force present in the deep-space environment, such as drag from interplanetary media or solar environmental pressure gradients, acts on the spacecraft along the Sun-pointing vector.
supporting_evidence: The directional vector of the acceleration residual is known to be approximately Sun-pointing (P-02).
The trajectory anomaly affects multiple deep-space spacecraft operating in similar regions of the solar system (P-01).
contradicting_evidence: The anomaly is observed specifically in spacecraft sharing similar physical design characteristics (P-01, P-04), which favors an internal design-dependent origin over a universal environmental effect.
Standard gravitational and known environmental forces are already modeled in precision trajectory fits (P-01, P-08).
Available evidence is insufficient to verify the presence of an interplanetary medium of sufficient density to produce the observed force magnitude.
hypotheses.discriminating_test: Determine whether the acceleration residual vector remains fixed toward the Sun regardless of changes in the spacecraft's physical attitude and spin-axis orientation (P-02, P-06).

key_unknowns: Precise directional vector of the residual acceleration (whether aligned strictly with the spin axis, Sun direction, Earth direction, or velocity vector) (P-02, P-06).
Whether the observed temporal correlation between radioisotope decay and the trajectory residual rate of change reflects direct physical causation or an unmodeled coincidence (P-04, P-07).
Detailed thermal emission and reflection coefficients for the specific structural materials and geometry of the spacecraft (P-04, P-05).
recommended_next_tests: Perform vector alignment analysis comparing trajectory residuals against spacecraft spin-axis orientation versus Sun/Earth directional vectors over time (P-02, P-06).
Execute comprehensive finite-element thermal radiation pressure modeling using internal heat decay data to calculate expected net thrust (P-04, P-05, P-07).
Evaluate propulsion system telemetry for evidence of asymmetric mass loss or propellant leakage (P-01, P-04).

main_weaknesses: Temporal correlation between internal radioisotope thermal decay and residual acceleration changes (P-04, P-07) is assumed to be causal without quantitative physical modeling.
Existing standard force models have not yet demonstrated complete numerical resolution of the observed residual magnitude purely from thermal radiation (P-01, P-08).
The directional vector of the acceleration residual remains ambiguous between a spacecraft-fixed frame (spin axis) and an external reference frame (P-02, P-06).
unsupported_assumptions: Assumes asymmetric heat reflection off structural geometry produces net directional recoil thrust of sufficient magnitude to account for the residual.
Assumes the temporal rate of change in the trajectory residual is driven by radioisotope decay rather than a coincidental decaying process (e.g., outgassing decay or environmental variation).
Assumes the spacecraft spin axis and Sun-pointing vector are sufficiently co-aligned such that an approximately Sun-pointing vector residual (P-02) represents spin-axis thrust.
evidence_that_would_falsify: High-fidelity finite-element thermal modeling demonstrating that net thermal radiation pressure accounts for significantly less than the observed trajectory residual magnitude.

Trajectory residual vector analysis during spacecraft orientation adjustments showing that the directional force vector stays fixed toward the Sun/Earth rather than rotating with the spacecraft spin axis (P-02, P-06).
Empirical measurement showing the residual temporal decay rate diverges significantly from the half-life and heat output curve of the radioisotope power sources (P-04, P-07).
critiques.alternative_explanation: The gradual change in acceleration over time could be caused by continuous exponential decay of volatile outgassing (H2) or spatial displacement through an external environmental gradient (H3), rendering the correlation with radioisotope power decay purely coincidental.

main_weaknesses: Requires two independent, distinct spacecraft to exhibit nearly identical propellant leakage rates, valve degradation dynamics, and mass expulsion directions across multi-year tracking intervals (P-01, P-04).
Lacks direct telemetry evidence confirming propulsion system mass loss, pressure drops, or active outgassing.
unsupported_assumptions: Assumes propulsion components or volatile structural materials on both spacecraft experience persistent, low-level mass loss over multi-year periods.
Assumes accidental leak vectors happen to align persistently along or near the spin axis / Sun-pointing direction across separate vehicles.
evidence_that_would_falsify: Propulsion telemetry showing completely stable propellant tank pressures and zero mass loss over long intervals where residual acceleration persists.
Demonstration that trajectory residuals remain identical across both spacecraft while propulsion telemetry exhibits vastly different pressure and valve behavior between the vehicles (P-01, P-04).
critiques.alternative_explanation: The residual acceleration is produced by continuous onboard thermal radiation pressure (H1) or external environmental drag (H3), neither of which relies on accidental hardware leaks across multiple spacecraft.

main_weaknesses: Fails to explain why the anomaly is selectively observed in deep-space spacecraft sharing specific physical design characteristics (P-01, P-04) rather than universally affecting all deep-space objects.

Standard gravitational and known environmental forces are already accounted for in precision trajectory models (P-01, P-08), requiring an unverified external mechanism with no supporting density measurements.
unsupported_assumptions: Assumes the presence of an unmodeled external interplanetary medium or force gradient capable of generating measurable force on deep-space spacecraft.
Assumes an external environmental force selectively mimics design-dependent characteristics across distinct spacecraft.
evidence_that_would_falsify: Vector analysis proving that the acceleration residual vector rotates in lockstep with changes in spacecraft spin-axis orientation, establishing an internal frame origin (P-02, P-06).
In-situ or particle density measurements establishing that the interplanetary medium density is orders of magnitude lower than required to generate the observed force residual.
critiques.alternative_explanation: The residual acceleration is caused by internal, design-dependent physical forces such as asymmetric heat rejection (H1) or mass outgassing (H2).

cross_hypothesis_comparison.main_reason: It aligns naturally with the shared physical design characteristics of both spacecraft and the temporal decay of onboard power sources (P-01, P-04, P-07), though it remains unproven until full quantitative thermal force calculations resolve the magnitude gap (P-01, P-08).
Provides a physical thrust mechanism, but relies on the highly improbable assumption of identical continuous leaks and orientations across two separate spacecraft (P-01, P-04).

Matches the approximate Sun-pointing vector (P-02), but contradicts evidence that the residual is specific to spacecraft sharing design traits (P-01, P-04) and lacks evidence for an external force medium.

critical_unknowns: Whether the exact directional vector of acceleration is fixed relative to the spacecraft body/spin axis or relative to external coordinates (Sun/Earth) (P-02, P-06).
Whether the quantitative magnitude of thermal radiation recoil calculated from geometry and internal heat models matches 100% of the observed acceleration residual (P-01, P-04, P-05, P-08).
Whether observed temporal decay rates reflect true physical causation tied to radioisotope power decay or a coincidental correlation (P-04, P-07).
The trajectory evidence is currently insufficient to uniquely confirm any single hypothesis without resolving vector orientation ambiguity and completing thermal modeling.
recommended_discriminating_tests: Vector Alignment vs Attitude Maneuver Test: Analyze trajectory residuals during spacecraft spin-axis reorientation maneuvers to determine if the acceleration vector rotates with the spacecraft body frame (falsifying H3) or stays fixed to the Sun vector (falsifying H1 and H2) (P-02, P-06).

Finite-Element Thermal Thrust Modeling: Perform detailed finite-element thermal modeling incorporating geometry, surface reflection properties, and decay curves of internal radioisotope power sources to calculate expected net thrust magnitude and direction (P-04, P-05, P-07, P-08).

Propulsion System Telemetry & Mass Balance Audit: Inspect historical pressure, temperature, and thruster telemetry to set an upper bound on non-gravitational acceleration from propellant leakage or outgassing (P-01, P-04).

selection.reason: Estimating the acceleration generated by anisotropic thermal radiation allows us to quantitatively test whether onboard thermal radiation recoil can account for the magnitude of the observed trajectory residual as proposed in H1.

inputs.note: The current blind case does not contain numerical thermal telemetry, so these values are demonstration parameters.
